title: Legacy Contacts on Major Accounts
body:
Legacy contacts are the people an account owner names in advance to manage, memorialize, or close an account after death or incapacity, and setting them is the single most useful digital-legacy step. The practice is: open each important account's legacy or trusted-contact setting, name a person who is trusted and reachable, tell that person they were named and what is expected, and record where the setting lives. A legacy contact named in advance can act; a family member without one often cannot, however close the relationship.

Grief is a poor time to discover that an account has no named contact, and the discovery is made exactly then.

The working method is setting legacy contacts on accounts. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List the accounts that matter most: mail, photos, social, financial
  2. Open each account's legacy or trusted-contact setting
  3. Name a trusted, reachable person for each account
  4. Tell each named person what is expected of them
  5. Record where each setting lives, without recording any password

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Important accounts listed; OK :: Legacy settings opened; OK :: Trusted persons named; OK :: Named persons told what is expected; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. It teaches the setting habit, and families with significant assets should seek professional advice. A common mistake is assuming a close relative automatically gains access, when accounts generally require a named contact or legal process. title: Writing a Digital Asset List
body:
Writing a digital asset list means inventorying accounts, devices, subscriptions, domains, and digital holdings in one place, without writing any password into the list itself. The list states what exists, where it lives, and who should receive or close it, while passwords live separately in a password manager or with a trusted arrangement. A list without secrets can be shared with an executor safely, while a list with passwords becomes a second vulnerability.

An executor cannot close what they cannot find, and a list is how finding becomes possible.

The working method is digital asset list without secrets. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List accounts, devices, subscriptions, domains, and digital holdings
  2. State for each item whether it should be kept, transferred, or closed
  3. Name the recipient or closer for each item
  4. Store the list where the executor can find it
  5. Keep all passwords out of the list itself, in a separate safe arrangement

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Accounts and holdings listed; OK :: Keep, transfer, or close decided per item; OK :: Recipient or closer named per item; OK :: No passwords in the list; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. An asset list is an inventory, not a legal instrument, and it does not transfer ownership by itself. Transfer and closure still follow each service's rules and applicable law, which this record does not interpret. A common mistake is writing passwords into the asset list, which turns an executor's guide into a master key. title: Passwords After Death: What Executors Can and Cannot Do
body:
Passwords after death are a subject where good intentions collide with account rules: using a deceased person's password to enter their accounts may breach the service's terms and, in some places, the law, even when the intention is benign. The lawful routes are legacy contacts, the service's deceased-user process, and court or estate processes where they apply. Executors should therefore plan with legacy contacts and service processes, not with shared passwords, and should never ask family members to impersonate the deceased online.

A password shared with love is still a password used without authority, and authority is what executors must establish properly.

The working method is executor password limits and lawful routes. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Set legacy contacts before they are needed
  2. Learn each important service's deceased-user process
  3. Do not use the deceased person's password to enter accounts
  4. Do not ask family to impersonate the deceased online
  5. Seek professional guidance where an account holds significant value or dispute

The output reads: OK :: Legacy contacts set in advance; OK :: Deceased-user processes learned; OK :: No password use after death; OK :: No impersonation requested; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. title: Memorialization Choices
body:
Memorialization choices decide what happens to a person's online presence after death: whether an account becomes a memorial page, is closed, or is left untouched, and who decides. The choice belongs, wherever possible, to the person while alive, recorded plainly and told to the legacy contact, because families left to guess often disagree, and disagreement in grief harms more than the choice itself. A memorial page can comfort, but it can also distress, and the choice should reflect the person's wishes, not only the family's comfort.

The kindest memorial is the one the person chose, and choosing requires being asked in time.

The working method is memorialization versus deletion choices. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Decide per account: memorialize, close, or leave untouched
  2. Record each choice plainly and tell the legacy contact
  3. Name who decides where no choice was recorded
  4. Consider who will see a memorial page and how it may affect them
  5. Review choices after major life changes

title: Photos and Memories: Who Keeps Them
body:
Photos and memories are often the digital legacy families value most, and the plan for them is: which photos matter, where the originals live, who receives copies, and how they will be preserved. The practice is to export important photos to a shared archive the family controls, name a keeper, and ensure the keeper has access that does not depend on the deceased person's password. Memories kept only in one account, behind one password, are memories at risk.

Families mourn people, and photographs are how mourning remembers faces, so their keeping deserves a plan.

The working method is photo and memory preservation planning. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Identify the photos and memories that matter most
  2. Export them to a family-controlled archive, not only one account
  3. Name a keeper who will preserve and share them
  4. Ensure the keeper's access does not depend on a deceased password
  5. Record the archive's location for the executor

title: Subscriptions After Death
body:
Subscriptions after death are the small recurring charges that continue quietly until someone cancels them: streaming, software, storage, memberships, and deliveries. The practice is to list every subscription with its billing method, name who cancels each one, and cancel promptly after death, since months of unnoticed charges add up and complicate estate accounts. The asset list is the tool for this job, and the subscription section deserves its own review.

Small charges are easy to overlook in grief, and overlooking them is exactly how they continue for a year.

The working method is subscription cancellation after death. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List every subscription with its billing method
  2. Name who cancels each subscription
  3. Cancel promptly after death, starting with the largest charges
  4. Check bank and card statements for subscriptions the list missed
  5. Keep cancellation confirmations with estate records

title: Digital Wills and Letters of Instruction
body:
Digital wills and letters of instruction are the documents that carry digital wishes into the estate: a will that mentions digital assets generally, and a letter of instruction that details accounts, choices, and contacts without containing passwords. The letter is updated more easily than a will, so it carries the changing details, while the will carries the durable authority. Both should be stored where the executor can find them, and the letter's existence should be told to the executor in life.

A will speaks in law, while a letter speaks in detail, and digital wishes need both voices.

The working method is digital wills and letters of instruction. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Ensure the will mentions digital assets generally
  2. Write a letter of instruction detailing accounts, choices, and contacts
  3. Keep all passwords out of both documents
  4. Store both where the executor can find them
  5. Tell the executor the letter exists, while alive

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Will mentions digital assets; OK :: Letter of instruction written; OK :: No passwords in either document; OK :: Executor told the letter exists; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Families should have wills prepared or reviewed by a qualified professional in their jurisdiction. A common mistake is putting passwords in the letter of instruction, which turns guidance into a master key. title: Business and Creator Accounts After Incapacity
body:
Business and creator accounts after incapacity need continuity planning, because audiences, customers, and income depend on accounts that may be personal in name but business in effect. The plan names a trusted person who can post a notice, pause activity, or transfer control, records which accounts are business-critical, and separates business credentials from personal ones in advance. Without a plan, a creator's silence is read as disappearance, and a business's silence loses customers it cannot afford to lose.

A business built on personal accounts is a business with a single point of failure, and that point is a person.

The working method is business and creator account continuity. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List business-critical accounts separately from personal ones
  2. Name a trusted person for notice, pause, or transfer
  3. Separate business credentials from personal credentials in advance
  4. Record what the trusted person may and may not do
  5. Review the plan when the business changes hands, tools, or platforms

title: Cryptocurrency and Digital Money After Death
body:
Cryptocurrency and digital money after death raise the sharpest legacy problem: self-held assets whose keys are lost are generally unrecoverable, while custodial assets follow the custodian's process. The plan is to inventory holdings without recording keys in the inventory, arrange lawful transfer through guardians, executors, or custodians as appropriate, and tell executors that holdings exist and where instructions live. The balance is delicate: instructions must be findable by the right person and useless to the wrong one, which is why keys and instructions must never travel together.

Digital money's freedom is also its legacy risk: no company can reset what only its owner held.

The working method is digital money inheritance education. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Inventory holdings without recording keys in the inventory
  2. Arrange transfer through guardians, executors, or custodians as appropriate
  3. Tell executors that holdings exist and where instructions live
  4. Keep keys and instructions separate at all times
  5. Review the arrangement whenever holdings or guardians change

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record was executed at build time, so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: OK :: Holdings inventoried without keys; OK :: Transfer route arranged; OK :: Executors told holdings exist; OK :: Keys and instructions kept separate; ok: 4/4; VERDICT: PASS - all checks ok. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. This record is education, not financial or legal advice, and digital-money inheritance law and tax treatment vary by jurisdiction and are developing. title: Domain Names and Websites After Death
body:
Domain names and websites after death need succession planning, because a domain that lapses can be taken by someone else, and a website that stops being paid for disappears. The plan lists domains, registrars, renewal dates, and hosting, names who renews or transfers each one, and decides which sites should be preserved, transferred, or allowed to lapse. Renewal dates deserve a calendar, since a lapsed domain is often unrecoverable at its original price.

A domain is rented ground, and rented ground is lost when the rent stops, however loved the building on it.

The working method is domain and website succession. Follow these steps in order:

  1. List domains, registrars, renewal dates, and hosting
  2. Name who renews or transfers each domain
  3. Decide per site: preserve, transfer, or allow to lapse
  4. Calendar renewal dates with reminders to the named person
  5. Record hosting access routes without recording passwords in the list

title: Medical and Health Records Access for Carers
body:
Medical and health records access for carers covers the permissions a carer needs when the patient cannot act: which records, which providers, and which legal permissions apply. The practice is to arrange permissions in advance, record which providers hold records, name the carer in each provider's system where possible, and keep a list of medications and conditions the carer can show in an emergency. Health privacy rules protect patients, so carer access must be arranged, not assumed.

In an emergency, a carer without arranged access is a stranger to the system, however close they are to the patient.

The working method is health record access for carers. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Arrange carer permissions in advance with each provider
  2. Record which providers hold which records

title: Incapacity Planning: Trusted Access Before Crisis
body:
Incapacity planning arranges trusted access before a crisis, so that a trusted person can act when the owner cannot, without impersonation and without delay. The arrangement combines legal permissions where they exist, legacy contacts where offered, and a letter of instruction that states what the trusted person may do. The hardest part is the conversation itself, which families postpone because it feels morbid, while postponement is exactly what turns a manageable incapacity into a crisis.

Trusted access arranged in calm is a gift; trusted access improvised in crisis is a legal problem.

The working method is incapacity trusted-access planning. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Have the trusted-access conversation while the owner can still decide
  2. Arrange legal permissions where they exist in the jurisdiction
  3. Set legacy contacts where services offer them
  4. Write a letter of instruction stating what the trusted person may do
  5. Review the arrangement after major health or family changes

title: Disputes: When Family and Platforms Disagree
body:
Disputes arise when family wishes, a deceased person's recorded choices, and a platform's rules point in different directions, and the handling skill is to proceed in order: the person's recorded choice first, then the platform's deceased-user process, then estate or legal process where needed, with all correspondence kept. Families should avoid public disputes about a memorial page or account, since publicity hardens positions and harms grieving people, and should seek mediation or professional advice before escalating.

In a dispute about the dead, the dead person's own recorded choice is the voice that should speak loudest.

The working method is family-platform dispute handling. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Start from the person's recorded choice, where one exists
  2. Follow the platform's deceased-user process next
  3. Keep all correspondence with dates and names
  4. Avoid public disputes about memorials or accounts
  5. Seek mediation or professional advice before escalating

title: Digital Legacy for Children and Dependents
body:
Digital legacy for children and dependents covers the accounts, photos, school records, and memories of a child or dependent person, and the question of who stewards them if a parent or carer dies or becomes incapacitated. The plan names a steward, records where photos and records live, states what may be shared and what must stay private, and respects that a child's digital life is not a parent's property to dispose of at will. The steward's duty is preservation with restraint, not publication.

A child's digital life deserves a steward, not an owner, and stewardship means restraint as much as care.

The working method is legacy planning for children and dependents. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Name a steward for the child's digital life
  2. Record where photos, records, and accounts live
  3. State what may be shared and what must stay private
  4. Ensure the steward's access does not depend on a deceased password
  5. Review the plan as the child grows and gains their own agency

title: Preserving a Life Story: Archives and Memorials
body:
Preserving a life story means gathering a person's writings, photos, recordings, and milestones into an archive that outlives any single account, with a named keeper and a stated audience. The practice is to choose what to preserve rather than saving everything, to include context such as dates and names, to store copies in more than one place, and to decide what stays private within the family and what may be shared publicly. An archive without a keeper decays like any other unattended collection.

A life story preserved without context is a box of faces without names, and context is what turns files into memory.

The working method is life story archive and memorial preservation. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Choose what to preserve, rather than saving everything
  2. Add context: dates, names, places, and relationships
  3. Store copies in more than one place
  4. Name a keeper and state the audience
  5. Decide what stays private and what may be shared publicly

title: Annual Digital Legacy Review
body:
An annual digital legacy review keeps the whole plan true: accounts opened and closed, legacy contacts changed, asset lists updated, memorial choices revisited, and the executor told of changes. The review is short when done yearly and painful when postponed for years, because accounts multiply silently and contacts drift. The review ends by setting next year's date and telling the executor that the plan was reviewed, so the executor knows the plan is current, not merely old.

A legacy plan is a living document, and living documents die when they stop being reviewed.

The working method is annual digital legacy review. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Update the account and asset list for openings and closures
  2. Review legacy contacts and named stewards
  3. Revisit memorial choices after life changes
  4. Update the letter of instruction and tell the executor
  5. Set next year's review date before finishing
